insights.title: Flow speed controls flame spread over solids — BASS / BASS-II (250 tests)
insights.text: BASS and BASS-II burned Japan wax, Nomex, PMMA, SIBAL, Ultem, paraffin wax, wax in the ISS glovebox flow duct (250 test rows; BASS-II O2 13.6–22.2 %). Quoted results on how airflow speed sets spread rate and extinction:

numbers.mats: Japan wax, Nomex, PMMA, SIBAL, Ultem, paraffin wax, wax

citations.quote: The effects of air flow speed on flame appearance, flame growth, and spread rates were determined in both the opposed and concurrent-flow configuration.

In addition, by decreasing concurrent-flow speed to a very low value (around 1 cm/s), quenching extinction was observed providing a direct verification of the theoretically predicted U-shaped flammability boundary for a thin fuel.

Depending on the flow speed, the flame would either spread entirely into the flow (opposed flow) or the ignition flame would split into an opposed and concurrent-flow flame spreading simultaneously away from each other.

insights.title: 1 g material screening (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) vs microgravity — checked by 5 investigations
insights.text: BASS, BASS-II and Saffire I–III were designed to compare NASA's 1 g upward-burning screening test with actual flammability in low gravity. Quoted statements:

citations.quote: It will also provide an increased margin of safety for materials flammability based upon a slightly modified NASA Test 1 protocol, since recent drop-tower results suggest that the current Test 1 might not be conservative.
Radiant heat transfer was shown to substantially affect the material’s flammability.

insights.title: Large-scale fire growth in a real spacecraft — Saffire I–III (13 samples, 20–30 cm/s)
insights.text: Saffire I–III burned SIBAL, PMMA, PMMA + Nomex, silicone inside an uncrewed Cygnus vehicle at 20–30 cm/s airflow and ~21.5–22.1 % O2 (13 sample rows). Quoted statements:

citations.quote: The sample material for Saffire-I is a composite fabric called Sibal consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight).
The fuels and sample materials tested in SAFFIRE-II (PSI-99) were: PMMA, PMMA + Nomex, SIBAL, silicone (solid fuels).
As a follow on to the Saffire-I investigation, the Saffire-II investigation added more samples including SIBAL, silicone, structure PMMA, flat PMMA, and PMMA with Nomex.

insights.title: Burning at elevated O2 — ACME BRE solid-fuel emulator (21–40 % O2, 18 test days)
insights.text: ACME BRE used a gas burner that emulates burning solids at 21–40 % O2 (18 test-day rows) — the only PSI flight data reaching exploration-atmosphere O2 for solid-like fuels. Quoted results:

citations.quote: This is a profound result indicating a common plastic could steadily burn under these NASA proposed atmospheric conditions.

In summary, the following conditions are selected: • Atmospheric pressure: 0.56 and 1 bar • Atmospheric oxygen mole fraction: 021, 0.265 0.34 and 0.40, representing NASA considered atmospheres [65,92]. • Material heat of combustion: 23.6 and 47.2 kJ/g, representing a wide range of plastics.
Generally, it has been found that oxygen levels of 26 % and above can allow steady flames.

insights.title: Smoke particle size in microgravity — SAME / SAME-R (117 tests)
insights.text: SAME and SAME-R heated Kapton, Teflon, dibutyl phthalate, lampwick, silicone, Pyrell on the ISS and measured the smoke (117 test rows). Quoted results on particle size and what it means for detectors:

numbers.mats: Kapton, Teflon, dibutyl phthalate, lampwick, silicone, Pyrell

citations.quote: In combination with the knowledge gained from prev ious CSD experiment, it becomes obvious that the detection of smoke across the size range seen in SA ME and CSD, while still discriminating against dust (which tends to be large), will prob ably require a detection system that can discriminate the particle size distribution to at least a limited degree.

These figures were developed assuming the alarm level was set at 2 mg/m 3 for a log-normal particle size distribution with a 500 nm geometric mean diameter (GMD) and a geometric standard deviation (GSD) of 1.3.

Considering the results from both the SAME and CSD experiments, the only two fire detection experiments conducted in low-gravity, broader smoke particulate size distributions can be produced from credible pre-fire overheat events, depending on the conditions.

insights.title: Ionization vs light-scattering smoke detection — 6 detector / counter types flown in SAME
insights.text: SAME / SAME-R flew 6 smoke-detector and particle-counter types side by side (from the profiles' instrument lists). Quoted results on which ones saw the smoke:

citations.quote: All of the tests conducted in this series of experiments showed strong signals on the Space Shuttle detector (ionization) despite the larger particle si ze distributions seen for the lamp wick(cellulose) and silicone rubber.

Space Shuttle Detectors At the time the Space Shuttle Orbiter (Space Transportation System (STS)) was developed, smoke detection for terrestrial applications was becoming commonplace. 2 In particular, ionization detectors were becoming readily available but photoelectric (scattering or obscuration detectors) were generally unavailable due to the difficulty of producing stable light sources.
Light scattering devices are most sensitive to particulate whose size is of the same order as the wavelength of the light used by the detector, typically particle diameters greater than 0.3 μm.

insights.title: Dust vs smoke on orbit — DAFT particle-counter test (2 test rows)
insights.text: DAFT / DAFT-2 flew a TSI P-Trak particle counter with test dust (2 test rows). Quoted results on how dust behaves without gravity:

citations.quote: This observation makes sense since, on-orbit, without gravity to drive settling, more of the larger particles from the dust sample should remain entrained.

insights.title: Droplet flames: heptane burned to completion down to 14 % O2 — FLEX (274 tests)
insights.text: FLEX (274 droplet tests, O2 12–34 %, 70–309 kPa): lowest O2 with burn-to-completion was 14 % (heptane) and 18 % (methanol); flames extinguished at 13–24 % (heptane, 60 tests) and 12–30 % (methanol, 126 tests). Quoted findings on the limiting oxygen index:

citations.quote: This oxygen concentration is called the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI ).
The research to date has shown that the flammability limit is lower in reduced gravity.

Instead of observing flame extinction, however, the procedure involved an iterative sequence of tests (burn to completion followed by a no ignition test) with progressively smaller increments in ambient oxygen mole fraction to determine the LOI .

insights.title: CO2 and helium as suppressants — FLEX (123 CO2 tests, 50 He tests)
insights.text: FLEX added CO2 (up to 70% mole fraction, 123 tests) or helium (up to 45%, 50 tests) to the ambient. Quoted statements on how the suppressant changes the extinction limit:

citations.file: documents/PSI-68/PSI-68_Science Documents_FLEX-2 SRD Final _ No Hypertext .pdf
citations.quote: The helium and nitrogen-diluted microgravity experiments clearly exhibit diﬀerent extinction behavior for the binary arrays versus the single droplets.

The hot ﬂame extinguished quickly for the higher ambient helium mole fraction test and the cool ﬂame burning period was also short with the cool ﬂame extinction droplet diameter larger than the hot ﬂame extinction droplet diameter for the test with the smaller ambient helium mole fraction.

insights.title: Each 1 % less O2 → flame out at a 0.11 mm larger droplet (FLEX model, n=188)
insights.text: Linear model on 188 FLEX tests (5-fold CV R² 0.72, RMSE 0.52 mm): extinction diameter rises 0.11 mm per percentage point less O2, other inputs fixed (`ai.model.predict_flex`). Quoted statements on extinction diameter:

citations.file: documents/PSI-68/PSI-68_Science Documents_FLEX-2 SRD Final _ No Hypertext .pdf
citations.quote: In the 0.15 oxygen mole fraction ambient, the ﬂame surrounding the binary array always extinguished at a ﬁnite droplet size that was larger than the single droplet extinction diameter.
In FLEX (PSI-69), the flame was extinguished in 186 tests run at oxygen (O2) concentrations of 12 to 30 percent.

Instead of observing flame extinction, however, the procedure involved an iterative sequence of tests (burn to completion followed by a no ignition test) with progressively smaller increments in ambient oxygen mole fraction to determine the LOI .

insights.title: Cool flames can keep burning after the visible flame goes out — FLEX / CFI (361 tests)
insights.text: FLEX and CFI droplet tests (361 rows) recorded low-temperature 'cool flames' after visible flame extinction — relevant when judging whether a fire is really out. Quoted results:

citations.quote: The FLEX experiments performed to date demonstrated radiative and diffusive extinction, combustion instabilities, lower flammability limits and recently explained cool flame phenomenon after visible flame extinction.
The pure heptane droplet radiatively extinguishes and then has a prolonged period of cool ﬂame burning with the cool ﬂame extinguishing at a droplet diameter slightly larger than 1 mm.
This vaporization, we now know, is supported by a lower-temperature cool flame that forms after visible flame extinction.

insights.title: No partial-gravity (Moon 1/6 g, Mars 3/8 g) combustion data in PSI — and 0 g / 1 g results may not bound it.
insights.text: All 19 flight investigations ran in microgravity; ACME E-FIELD (PSI-22) uses electric fields only as a proxy. The challenge text says 0 g and 1 g results 'could bound' partial gravity, but that is not guaranteed: in microgravity, concurrent flame spread is most vigorous at an intermediate, low flow speed (the 'Goldilocks' flammability zone of Olson and Ferkul, PSI-62), and the weak buoyant flow at lunar or Martian gravity is also low speed, so a partial-gravity case could be worse than both. Planned NASA experiments LUCI and FM2 are meant to measure it.

Generally, the convective flows driven by electric fields acting on flame ions and those driven by buoyancy have been found to be of the same order of magnitude in earth gravity.
